events.title: The death of Pope Alexander VI
events.shortBlurb: Rodrigo Borgia, the ablest and most infamous of the Renaissance popes, died suddenly of fever, and his son's principality in the Romagna died with him…
body: Roderic de Borja was born at Xàtiva near Valencia on 1 January 1431, was made cardinal at twenty-five by his uncle Calixtus III, and for thirty-five years, as vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, served five popes with rare address. In August 1492 he was himself elected pope as Alexander VI, in a conclave tainted by promises and gifts.

His eleven years were spent in statecraft: he faced the French invasion of Charles VIII, excommunicated Savonarola, kept the jubilee of 1500, and by the bull Inter caetera of 1493 drew the line between Spanish and Portuguese discovery in the new world. For his children he was prodigal — Lucrezia in her marriages, Cesare in his carving of a duchy out of the Romagna — and the papal name sank to its lowest repute.

In the hot August of 1503 both father and son sickened after a dinner at a cardinal's villa near Rome. Cesare recovered; the pope died on 18 August, aged seventy-two. Men told of poison then and since, but the likelier cause was the Roman fever. Within months Pius III was dead in his turn and Julius II reigned, who broke Cesare and repaired what the Borgia had made his own.
